fields.meta_title: What Is Faith? Understanding Biblical Faith
fields.description: Biblical faith is not a leap in the dark but a settled trust in a trustworthy God. Here is what faith is, how it saves, and how a struggling faith grows.
fields.body_html:
Faith is the hinge on which the whole Christian life turns. We are saved by faith, we live by faith, we please God by faith — and yet ask ten people what faith actually is and you will get ten different answers. Some think it means believing things without evidence; others treat it as a vague optimism, a hope that things will work out. The Bible means something far more solid and far more relational. Biblical faith is not a leap into the dark but a trust in the light: a settled reliance on God and on the promises of God, grounded in his proven character. It is taking God at his word and acting accordingly.

Scripture’s own definition is the famous one from Hebrews: “Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith deals with realities we cannot yet see — but it treats them as certain, because the God who promised them is certain. Let us look more closely at what that means.

Faith is trust in a trustworthy God

Faith is not believing hard enough to make something true; it is resting on Someone who is already true. Its object matters more than its strength. A small faith in a great God accomplishes more than a great confidence in ourselves, because faith’s power lies not in the believer but in the One believed. That is why Jesus could say that faith the size of a mustard seed is enough to move mountains (Matthew 17:20) — the point is not the size of the seed but the greatness of the God it clings to.

So the ground of faith is God’s character. When Abraham was promised a son in old age, “he did not weaken in faith... No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:19–21). Notice the reasoning: Abraham was persuaded not because the circumstances looked promising — they looked impossible — but because he was convinced God could be trusted. Faith looks past the circumstances to the character of the One who spoke.

Faith comes by hearing God’s word

Faith is not something we conjure from within; it is a response to something God says. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). This is enormously practical. If your faith is weak, the way to strengthen it is not to strain harder but to steep yourself in the promises of God, for faith grows as it feeds on his word. The more clearly we hear what God has actually said, the more surely we can rest on it.

This also means faith is reasonable, not irrational. It is built on testimony — on what God has revealed and on what he has done in history, supremely in the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Faith is not a stubborn refusal to think; it is a considered trust in the most trustworthy witness there is. It says, with good reason, that the God who kept every promise in the past will keep his promises still.

Faith is how we are saved

At the centre of the gospel, faith is the empty hand that receives the free gift of God. We are not saved by our achievements but by trusting in Christ’s: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). Faith saves not because it is a good work that earns God’s favour, but precisely because it is the opposite of a work — it is the renouncing of our own merit and the resting of our whole weight on Christ.

This is why faith and grace fit together so perfectly. Grace is God freely giving; faith is the sinner simply receiving. “Whoever believes in him is not condemned” (John 3:18), Jesus said, and “whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). To believe, in this saving sense, is not merely to agree that Jesus existed, but to entrust yourself to him — to lean the full burden of your soul’s hope on him and on what he has done.

Faith is proved by how we live

Real faith is never merely an idea in the head; it shows itself in the life. James is blunt about it: “faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (James 2:17). This does not contradict salvation by faith alone; it clarifies what living faith looks like. A trust that never acts, never obeys, never risks anything on God’s word, is not the trust the Bible means. Genuine faith walks.

The great chapter on faith is really a chapter on faith’s actions: by faith Noah built, Abraham went out, Moses chose, and a host of others “through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises” (Hebrews 11:33). And Paul described his own daily life in the same terms: “the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Faith is not only how we start the Christian life; it is how we walk each step of it, for “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).

Yet even here, faith and works are not rivals. The works do not earn the salvation; they demonstrate that the faith is alive. A living tree bears fruit not in order to become a tree but because it is one. So the obedience that flows from faith is never an attempt to buy God’s favour — it is the natural evidence of a heart that already trusts him. Where there is no fruit at all, we may rightly ask whether there is any root; but the root is faith, and the fruit is its proof, never its price.

Faith honours God — and grows through testing

Of all the ways we relate to God, faith is the one that most delights him, because it takes him at his word and so treats him as the trustworthy God he is. “Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:6). To trust God is to honour him; to doubt his word is, however unintentionally, to call him unreliable.

Faith like this is often forged in trials. The stories that most strengthen the faith of others are usually the stories of people who trusted God for the impossible and watched him provide — who prayed rather than schemed, waited rather than grasped, and proved in hard places that God is faithful. Such lives are a standing witness that faith is not wishful thinking but a real transaction with a real and living God.

Faith is not a feeling

One of the most freeing things to learn is that faith is not the same as feeling faith-full. Feelings rise and fall with sleep and weather and news; faith rests on something steadier — the unchanging word of God. There will be days when God feels far away and the promises feel unreal. Faith is not the absence of those feelings but the decision to trust God’s word above them. The prophet Habakkuk reached the summit of faith not when everything flourished but when everything failed: “Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines... yet I will rejoice in the Lord; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:17–18).

This is faith at its purest — clinging to God when the evidence of the senses says nothing. Job reached the same place in his agony: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15). And the Psalmist, when his soul was cast down, preached to his own feelings rather than obeying them: “Why are you cast down, O my soul... Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5). Faith does not wait for the feelings to cooperate. It speaks God’s truth to the downcast heart and goes on trusting, and in time the feelings often follow the faith rather than leading it.

What to do with a small or struggling faith

If your faith feels weak, take heart: the Bible is full of people whose faith was mixed with doubt and who were received anyway. One desperate father cried to Jesus, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24) — and Jesus answered him. That honest prayer is one any struggling believer can pray. You do not need a perfect faith; you need a real one, however small, directed at the right Person.

And remember where faith finally rests: not on itself but on Jesus, “the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2). He is the one who gives faith, sustains it, and will bring it to completion. So feed your faith on his word, exercise it by obeying him, and when it falters, look away from your own believing to the One you believe in. The strength was never in the grip of your hand but in the One your hand is holding — and he will not let go.
